name: Marco Polo
summary: A Venetian merchant's son goes east at seventeen and comes home at forty-one. In a Genoese prison he dictates a book about Kublai Khan's empire, and that book carries Cathay, Quinsay and Cipangu onto European maps. Chinese records never name him, but they confirm things only someone who was there would know: the Persian envoys he sailed home with, and the Christian governor of Zhenjiang.

stops.note: Marco, aged 17, leaves with his father Niccolò and uncle Maffeo, who have been to Kublai's court once already. The Khan asked them for a hundred learned Christians and oil from the lamp of the Holy Sepulchre; with the papacy still vacant, they set out without waiting any longer.
The last crusader port in the Holy Land. They ask the papal legate, Teobaldo Visconti, for leave to fetch the oil.
Oil from the lamp of the Holy Sepulchre, as Kublai had asked.
The legate gives them letters for the Khan, explaining that there is still no pope.

The port of Lesser Armenia. News comes that the legate has been elected Pope Gregory X; recalled to Acre, they return with his blessing and two Dominican friars. The friars lose their nerve here when the Mamluks invade Armenia, and go home.
Turcomania, under the Mongols, where he says the finest carpets in the world are woven.
Greater Armenia: the best buckram in the world, and hot springs.
Past the mountain where Noah's ark is said to rest. He hears of a spring of oil near Baku, burned in lamps and rubbed on camels' mange.
The great market of the Ilkhanate, where merchants trade goods from India, Baghdad and Genoa.
He is shown the tombs of the three Magi, who he is told set out from here for Bethlehem.
A noble trading city that weaves a silk cloth called yazdi.
Turquoise mines, steel for weapons, and fine embroidery.
Raiders he calls Caraonas, who he says can darken the air by magic, fall on the caravan. The Polos escape to a village; most of their companions are killed or sold.
Old Hormuz, on the mainland. The ships are sewn with coconut twine, without iron nails, and they do not trust them; they turn back to go overland.
Back north by another road.
Mirrors of fine steel, and tutty, a zinc ointment for the eyes.
The plain of the Dry Tree, where he says Alexander fought Darius. Near here he tells the tale of the Old Man of the Mountain and his assassins.
The best melons in the world, cut in strips and dried in the sun.
'A noble city', still in ruins from the Mongol conquest. He says Alexander married Darius's daughter here.
Mountains made of salt, enough to supply the whole world.
Marco falls ill and recovers in the mountain air, over a year. Balas rubies and lapis lazuli are mined here.
Twelve days further up the Oxus, among people with a language of their own.
A high plain where fire burns poorly. The wild sheep with huge horns he describes are now called Marco Polo sheep.
Gardens, vineyards and cotton; Nestorian Christians live among the Muslims.
Many have swollen legs or goitres, which he blames on the water.
Cotton, flax and grain, traders and craftsmen. He does not mention the jade that had gone from these rivers to China for a thousand years.
Jasper and chalcedony in the rivers. A wife whose husband is away twenty days may take another husband.
An oasis in the sand. When an army passes, the people flee with their animals into the desert.
The last town before the desert. Travellers rest a week to load up for a month's crossing, warned of spirit voices that call men off the road.
A Buddhist oasis at the desert's edge. He describes the paper figures of men, horses and camels burned at funerals.
Rhubarb grows in the mountains here, and merchants carry it across the world.
They stay a year here on business he does not explain. Great monasteries hold reclining Buddhas, one of which still lies in Zhangye's Great Buddha Temple.
Yaks, and the musk deer, whose musk he describes in detail.
Camlets of white camel hair, the finest in the world.
Ruled by George, a Christian king of the Önggüt, whom he takes for an heir of Prester John.
A palace by a lake full of cranes, swans and partridges, where the Khan comes to hunt with his falcons.
Kublai's summer capital: a marble palace, and a cane palace held up by two hundred silk cords. The Khan welcomes them and takes to young Marco.

Kublai's new capital, Dadu. Marco learns several languages and goes on the Khan's errands, bringing back the news of strange lands that the Khan loves to hear. The book gives few dates for his seventeen years in China; those that follow are estimates.

A marble bridge over the Pulisanghin, Persian for 'stone bridge', 'so fine that it has few equals in the world'. He counts twenty-four arches; it has eleven. English speakers still call it the Marco Polo Bridge.
Here the roads part. One runs west through Cathay toward Tibet and Yunnan, which Marco took on an earlier mission; the other runs south-east toward Manzi, the old Song lands.
A city of silk, with a Nestorian church.
Salt is made here by boiling water drawn through salty earth.
Where a river is split in two, half flowing north toward Cathay and half south toward Manzi: the summit of the Grand Canal the Khan is digging.
Across the Caramoran, the Mongols' 'Black River', as they call the Yellow River, which then reached the sea by the Huai. On the far side lies Manzi.
A town on the dyke of the canal, rich in fish and game.
He claims to have governed the city for three years by the Khan's order. Chinese sources do not mention him, and many scholars doubt it.

Two Nestorian churches built by Mar Sargis, a Christian who governed the city for the Khan. A Chinese gazetteer of about 1333 confirms him: it names Mar Sargis and credits him with seven churches, six of them in and around Zhenjiang.
Six thousand stone bridges, he says, and so much silk that everyone is dressed in it.
'The finest and noblest city in the world'. Quinsay is xingzai, the 'temporary capital' of the fallen Song. He counts twelve thousand bridges, ten great markets, and a lake ringed with palaces.
South-west into the hills toward Fujian.
Handsome stone bridges, ginger and galingale, and hens with fur instead of feathers: silkie chickens.
A port where ships bring pearls and precious stones from the Indies, and sugar is made in great quantities.

One of the two greatest ports in the world, he says. Fourteen ships sail from here with the princess Kököchin, a bride for the Ilkhan Arghun of Persia. In 1941 the historian Yang Zhijiu found a Yuan post-station document of 1290 that names her three Persian envoys just as Polo does: Oulatai, Apusca and Coja.
Marco had been here before, in 1285, on the Khan's errand. Its king pays tribute in elephants and has, he says, 326 children.
Two islands he calls Sondur and Condur; later sailors knew them as Pulo Condore.
The channel is so shallow that ships must draw up their rudders.
Five months waiting for the monsoon, behind a stockade against the man-eaters he says live inland. He calls Sumatra 'Java the Less', and here the Pole Star sinks out of sight.
Islands where people go naked; red sandalwood and coconuts.

The finest rubies in the world, and a mountain with Adam's footprint, which Buddhists say is the Buddha's. He tells the Buddha's life and says that, had he been a Christian, he would have been a great saint.
Pearl divers of the Gulf of Mannar, who pay a tenth to the king and a share to the charmers who keep the sharks away.
Here the Pole Star, lost since Java, is seen again.
Pepper, brazilwood and the best indigo. From here he describes the ports up the Malabar coast, Tana, Cambay and Somnath, perhaps from calls on the way.
Of the six hundred who sailed, he says, only eighteen survive, the princess among them. Arghun has died, and she is married instead to his son Ghazan.
Nine months at the court of the Ilkhan Gaykhatu, who gives them four golden tablets for safe passage. News arrives that Kublai Khan has died.
Robbed of part of their goods.
Through the Bosporus toward home.
A Venetian island on the way home.
Home after 24 years. A later story says their relatives did not know them until they slit open the seams of their ragged coats and jewels spilled out.

A prisoner of the Genoese, perhaps after the battle of Curzola, he dictates his book to a fellow prisoner, the romance writer Rustichello of Pisa. Freed in 1299, he lives on in Venice as a merchant. On his deathbed in 1324, urged to take back its fables, he is said to have answered that he had not told half of what he saw.

informs.note: Cipangu, an island of gold, by report
